title: Bring me your mind
hook: Huike asks Bodhidharma to put his mind at peace; Bodhidharma says, bring it here

segments.voice: Yesterday, an emperor's list of good deeds, and Bodhidharma's answer. Your line: a kindness with no scoreboard. Did you manage one kindness with no scoreboard running? Day nine hundred thirteen.

Snow is falling. A man stands outside a monastery, waiting. Inside, the monk he has come to see sits facing a wall and doesn't turn around. The man is Huike. He has come a long way with one trouble, the kind that follows a person from room to room. When at last he speaks, he doesn't ask a clever question. He says: my mind isn't at peace. Please, teacher, settle it for me. Today, the answer he got.
screen: `SNOW, AND A MAN WAITING.` → `A MONK WHO WON'T TURN AROUND.` → `MY MIND ISN'T AT PEACE.`

segments.voice: First, the request. The Gateless Gate, a collection of Chan stories with short comments, tells this as one of its cases. Huike's words are simple enough for anyone to say at three in the morning: my mind is not at peace; please pacify it. Second, the answer. Bodhidharma doesn't offer advice or a technique. He says: bring me your mind, and I'll pacify it for you. Hand it over. Put it on the table. Third, the search. Huike looks. And he says: I've searched for my mind, and I can't find it. Bodhidharma answers: there, I have pacified it for you. That's the whole exchange. Chan remembers Huike as the student who received Bodhidharma's teaching, the second ancestor in its line. Fourth, what happened in that search. Huike was asked to do something odd: not to fix his mind, but to find it. When you go looking for the anxious mind, you find things: a thought about tomorrow, a tight feeling in the chest, a picture of someone's face, a sentence repeating itself. But they keep moving. You can't pick the whole thing up and hand it to anyone. Some readers hear Bodhidharma saying the trouble was never a solid object; others hear a teacher simply turning a student around to look. Either way, the peace in the story doesn't come from a new answer. It comes from looking straight at the question. When worry feels like a heavy thing to carry, this story offers a small experiment: go and find it.
screen: `MY MIND IS NOT AT PEACE.` · `BRING ME YOUR MIND.` · `I'VE SEARCHED AND CAN'T FIND IT.` · `LOOKING STRAIGHT AT THE WORRY.` · then, large: `I CAN'T FIND IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for your anxious mind. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring up one small worry, not the biggest one. Let it be there. Now, gently, go looking for the mind that's worried. Where is it? In the head? The chest? Does it have a shape, an edge, a color? Each time you find a thought, notice it's already moving, and look again. No need to force an answer. If the worry softens, let it. If it doesn't, keep looking with curiosity. The bell holds the time.
Huike. The student who asked Bodhidharma to pacify his mind, and found, when he looked for it, that he couldn't. Today's word.
Your line: I can't find it. Today, when a worry shows up, pause and go looking for it, just for a breath or two. Day nine hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Chan and Zen students study the exchange between Bodhidharma and Huike as a koan, and meditation teachers in several traditions invite students to turn and look directly at the mind that worries.
